changes.before: Complete shift_date(day_text, days). Parse valid YYYY-MM-DD text, move it by the supplied integer number of days, and return YYYY-MM-DD text. Zero and negative day offsets are allowed. Inputs are valid calendar dates; no current clock or timezone is involved.
changes.after: Move a calendar date forward or backward by a given number of days.

before: datetime contains tools for calendar dates and times. This lesson uses date for a calendar day, not a moment with a timezone.
from datetime import date, timedelta imports the two tools. date.fromisoformat("2026-04-30") reads year-month-day text into a date value.
timedelta(days=1) represents a one-day difference. Adding it to a date follows calendar boundaries instead of adding to the characters in a string.

```python
from datetime import date, timedelta
day = date.fromisoformat("2026-04-30")
later = day + timedelta(days=1)
print(later.isoformat())
```
The result is 2026-05-01. isoformat converts the date back to year-month-day text.
A negative days value moves backward; zero keeps the same day. Leap years also matter: the day after 2024-02-28 is 2024-02-29.
Use the function’s supplied days value rather than always adding one. Each call returns new text; it does not change the input string.
Calendar dates alone do not settle timezone or daylight-saving questions about exact moments. Those require a separate time-aware design.
